summary: Montenegro lies in the southwest of the Balkan Peninsula on the Adriatic coast; its name means "Black Mountain", and in 2006 it became independent from its union with Serbia.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: From 1516 to 1851 Montenegro was ruled by the Orthodox prince-bishops of Cetinje, who were also secular rulers, and Orthodoxy was closely bound up with the national identity of resistance to the Ottoman Empire. Today most Orthodox Christians belong to the Serbian Orthodox Church, but from the 2000s another unrecognized body, the Montenegrin Orthodox Church, has claimed autocephaly; the 2019 religion law passed by the government triggered large-scale protests, reflecting divisions in national identity.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: During Ottoman rule of the Balkans (15th–19th centuries), some Slavs and Albanians converted to Islam. Today Muslims are mainly Bosniaks and people who call themselves Muslims in the northern Sandžak region (such as Rožaje and Plav), and Albanians in places such as Ulcinj in the south.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism is found mainly in the coastal Bay of Kotor region, which was ruled by the Republic of Venice from 1420 to 1797 and kept the Catholic faith, with a mostly Croat population; in addition, some Albanians are also Catholic.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: In Montenegro religion and national identity are closely bound together, and very few explicitly call themselves non-religious. Secularization in the socialist Yugoslav period affected some people, but religious identity has clearly revived since independence.

religion.background: In the Middle Ages Montenegro was part of the Kingdom of Serbia, and Orthodoxy became the main faith from the 12th century. At the end of the 15th century the Ottoman Empire conquered the Balkans, but Montenegro's mountains remained semi-autonomous, and from 1516 to 1851 the Orthodox bishops of Cetinje also served as rulers (prince-bishops), uniting religion and politics. During Ottoman rule some inhabitants converted to Islam, while the coastal Bay of Kotor remained Catholic under the Republic of Venice. In 1918 it was merged into Yugoslavia, and it became independent after a referendum in 2006. After independence the dispute between the Montenegrin Orthodox Church and the Serbian Orthodox Church became an important issue of national identity.

language.official: Montenegrin is the official language; Serbian, Bosnian, Albanian and Croatian are also officially recognized.

ranking.name: Serbian
ranking.description: In the Yugoslav period the language spoken by Montenegrins was called Serbo-Croatian, and many considered themselves Serbs or identified closely with Serbia. After independence in 2006, a large number of residents (especially pro-Serbian groups) still call their mother tongue Serbian, so Serbian has the most speakers in the census.

ranking.name: Montenegrin
ranking.description: Montenegrin became an official language in the 2007 constitution, and in 2009 a standard was drawn up and two letters (ś, ź) were added to reflect local pronunciation. Those who support independence and Montenegrin national identity tend to call their mother tongue Montenegrin, so this proportion reflects identity rather than actual linguistic differences.

ranking.name: Bosnian
ranking.description: Bosnian speakers are mainly the Bosniaks (Muslim Slavs) of the northern Sandžak region, who converted to Islam in the Ottoman period and, after the 1990s, named their language Bosnian to express national identity.

ranking.name: Albanian
ranking.description: Albanian speakers live mainly in Ulcinj in the south and in the eastern border areas, which are close to Albania and Kosovo, where Albanians have lived since the Middle Ages. Albanian is one of the official languages in the areas where they are concentrated.

language.history: The language of Montenegro belongs to the Shtokavian dialect of the South Slavic branch and is basically mutually intelligible with Serbian, Croatian and Bosnian. In the Yugoslav period these languages were collectively called "Serbo-Croatian". After the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, each country named its language according to national identity. After Montenegro became independent in 2006, the 2007 constitution made "Montenegrin" the official language and in 2009 a new standard was drawn up, adding two letters. But many residents still call their language Serbian, and the name of the language has become a symbol of national identity and political stance.

ranking.name: Njeguški pršut (Njeguši ham)
ranking.description: Raw ham made from pork hind legs salt-cured, smoked and air-dried in sea breezes and cold mountain air, eaten in thin slices. It has a light smoky aroma and a salty, delicate taste.
ranking.history: Njeguški pršut comes from the village of Njeguši in the Lovćen mountain area, the birthplace of Montenegro's Petrović-Njegoš dynasty. Njeguši lies between the mountains and the coast, where the warm sea breezes of the Adriatic meet the cold mountain air, creating a unique climate suited to air-drying ham. It is Montenegro's most representative specialty, often served as an appetizer with Njeguši cheese and local red wine.

ranking.name: Kačamak
ranking.description: A thick, porridge-like dish cooked by stirring cornmeal or potatoes with cheese and butter for a long time. It has a thick, creamy texture with the aroma of cheese and butter.
ranking.history: Kačamak is a traditional dish of the herders of the Montenegrin mountains; after corn reached the Balkans via the Ottoman Empire in the 16th–17th centuries it became an important staple of mountain farmers. In the cold mountains, a high-calorie dish made of corn, cheese and butter replenishes strength. Traditionally it needs to be stirred for a long time with a wooden spoon, and it is a representative dish of the mountains of northern Montenegro.

ranking.name: Burek
ranking.description: A flaky pastry pie of many thin layers of dough filled with cheese, minced meat or spinach and baked, often eaten with yogurt for breakfast. The crust is crisp and the fillings varied, and it is the most common breakfast in Montenegro.
ranking.history: Burek comes from the Ottoman börek and entered the Balkans with the Ottoman Empire after the 15th century. In Montenegro burek is the most common breakfast, with bakeries selling it from early morning, often with a glass of yogurt drink. It is one of the culinary legacies of Ottoman rule and is very widespread throughout the former Yugoslavia.

ranking.name: Ćevapi
ranking.description: Small sausages shaped from a mixture of ground beef and lamb, grilled over charcoal and served in flatbread with raw onion and kajmak. They are charred outside and juicy inside, a common grilled-meat dish.
ranking.history: Ćevapi derive from the grilled meat of the Ottoman Empire (kebab) and came to the Balkans with Ottoman rule in the 16th–17th centuries; Sarajevo in Bosnia is regarded as the birthplace of the modern ćevapi. In Montenegro it is one of the most common grilled-meat dishes, shared with former Yugoslav countries such as Serbia and Bosnia.

ranking.name: Kajmak
ranking.description: A rich cream cheese made by boiling milk, letting the milk fat on the surface set, then collecting and fermenting it, often spread on bread or eaten with grilled meat.
ranking.history: The name kajmak comes from Turkic, reflecting Ottoman culinary influence in the Balkans. Herders in the Montenegrin mountains make kajmak from cow's and sheep's milk because it keeps for a long time and is an important source of fat for mountain dwellers. Today it is an important accompaniment at breakfast and with grilled meat in Montenegro and Serbia, and traditionally it is made at home by the women of the household.
